Performance and mechanism of various microaerobic pretreatments on 
anaerobic digestion of tobacco straw 
Ligong Wang, Wenxiong Jin, Fanfan Cai, Chao Song, Yan Jin, Guangqing Liu, Chang Chen * 
College of Chemical Engineering, Beijing University of Chemical Technology, Beijing 100029, China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• Effects of various microaerobic pre­
treatments on AD of tobacco straw were 
studied. 
• Biogas slurry as pretreatment agent 
dosing 4 mL/g VS of O2 (BS-4) per­
formed better. 
• BS-4 had a good performance in the 
lignocellulosic decomposition of to­
bacco straw. 
• O2 dosing in microbial pretreatment 
process could change the microbial 
diversity.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Oxygen concentration 
Microbial pretreatment 
Methane yield 
Microbial community 
A B S T R A C T   
Tobacco straw is an abundant biomass in China’s agricultural ecosystems, and has high potential for methane 
production. However, the anaerobic digestion (AD) efficiency is limited by the recalcitrant lignocellulose 
structure of the tobacco straw. In this study, three microaerobic pretreatments were performed for the AD of 
tobacco straw to increase methane production. Among them, microbial pretreatment with biogas slurry at an 
oxygen concentration of 4 mL/g VS resulted in the highest methane production of 349.1 mL/g VS, increasing by 
19.8 % than that of untreated. During this pretreatment, the relative abundances of Enterococcus and Clostridium 
sensu stricto 12, which are closely related to acetic acid production and cellulose degradation, were high, and 
these bacteria might have an important contribution to substrate hydrolysis and the methanogenesis efficiency of 
the AD process. This study advances the understanding of microaerobic pretreatment processes and provides 
technological guidance for the efficient utilization of tobacco straw.   
1. Introduction 
Tobacco plays an important role in China’s economy, due to the first 
planting area and output worldwide. Based on the Statista data, the 
estimated tobacco production in 2022 is approximately 2.19 million 
metric tons. Zhang et al. (2023) had reported that tobacco straw ac­
counts for more than 48 % of tobacco production. As a result, over 1.05 
million metric tons of tobacco straw are generated a year and are either

abandoned or burned in fields, which not only results in a wastage of 
biomass resources but also leads to severe environment pollution. On the 
other hand, the tobacco mosaic virus and nicotine in tobacco straw make 
straw return and composting greatly challenging, as these components 
may migrate into the soil to decrease the yield and quality of tobacco for 
the next season. Therefore, a disposal measure that is effective and eco- 
friendly must be developed. 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) refers to the process in which anaerobic 
and facultative microorganisms transform biodegradable organics into 
methane and carbon dioxide through a series of biochemical reactions 
under oxygen-free conditions. Due to its low cost and environmental 
advantages, AD has frequently served as a method to recycle agricultural 
wastes. Like conventional agricultural residues, tobacco straw is pro­
duced in large quantities and is abundant in lignocellulose components. 
Therefore, tobacco straw may function as an effective supplement to 
existing feedstocks, but the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic structure 
presents a bottleneck for the utilization of the available organic matter 
in tobacco straw. 
Pretreatment strategies, such as physical and chemical pre­
treatments, are indicated measures to reduce the naturally recalcitrant 
structure of lignocellulosic biomass and increase hydrolysis rate. While a 
good consequence is received, the investment of physical and chemical 
pretreatments on the equipment and chemical reagent is relatively high, 
which may bring significant difficulties for commercial practice (Chen 
et al., 2022). Recently, microaerobic pretreatment achieved by intro­
ducing a small amount of oxygen or air into a pretreatment reactor 
before AD has gradually attracted increasing attention due to its ease of 
operation, low cost, and potential effectiveness (Huili˜nir et al., 2023). To 
the best of our knowledge, good AD performance after microaerobic 
pretreatment has been established for corn straw (Zhen et al., 2021), 
giant grass (Wang et al., 2021), rice straw (Amin et al., 2021b), and so 
on, but negative outcomes also exist (Díaz et al., 2011; Lim and Wang, 
2013; Okuda et al., 2007). The effect of microaerobic pretreatment 
varies with feedstock, and little research has been conducted to provide 
insights with respect to the pretreatment of tobacco straw. Considering 
the uniqueness of tobacco straw, gaps related to the impacts of micro­
aerobic pretreatment on AD should be addressed for the effective 
disposal and renewable energy generation of tobacco straw. 
Overall, the aims of this study are to (1) offer cost-effective pre­
treatment strategies using various microbial consortia to increase 
methane production from tobacco straw, (2) identify the effects of 
different microaerobic pretreatments on the concentration variations in 
volatile fatty acids (VFAs), the kinetics of methane generation, and 
lignocellulosic structural alterations, and (3) evaluate the mechanisms 
of microbial responses to oxygen from the pretreatment process to the 
AD stage. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Feedstocks and inoculum 
Tobacco straw was obtained from a farm in Hebei Province. A 
chopper was used to process the straw to a length of approximately 1 cm, 
and a cutting mill was employed to reduce its size to approximately 0.5 
mm prior to usage. Liquid inoculant (LI) and straw composting inoculant 
(SI) were commercially available for straw composting. The biogas 
slurry (BS) and inoculum were taken from a biogas plant in Beijing and 
subsequently digested for 2 weeks at room temperature to eliminate 
residual fermentable organic substances and release background 
methane. 
2.2. Microaerobic pretreatment and anaerobic digestion 
The microaerobic pretreatment experiment was carried out in 500 
mL serum bottles with the working volume of 150 mL. First, 1 g of LI, SI, 
and BS was added to the reactor to pretreat 5 g of tobacco straw (on a 
volatile solids (VS) basis), and subsequently, deionized water was added 
until a working volume of 150 mL was reached. Then, the pretreatment 
reactors were flushed with high-purity nitrogen for 3–4 min and care­
fully sealed to remove background air. Afterwards, different amounts (0, 
4, 8, 12, and 16 mL/g VS) of oxygen were introduced into the respective 
pretreatment groups to create the different microaerobic environments, 
and this atmosphere was maintained for 2 days at 37 ◦C. To simplify 
sample labeling, the sample microbially pretreated with SI at the oxygen 
concentration of 0 mL/g VS was labelled SI-0, and the names of the other 
groups were abbreviated in a similar way. The pretreatment experiment 
was performed in triplicate, and the reactors were manually mixed every 
4 h for uniform blending. 
AD was carried out after oxygen was completely consumed in each 
reactor. The organic loading and feed-to-inoculum ratio were 20 g VS/L 
and 1:1, respectively, and the working volume for AD was altered to 250 
mL. Thus, the inoculum was added for the AD reactor until the amount 
in each reactor reached 20 g VS/L, and then deionized water was added 
according to the working volume of 250 mL. The control groups con­
tained the pretreatment agent and inoculum were set to exclude 
methane production from the microbial agent, and untreated groups 
containing tobacco straw, inoculum, and the pretreatment agent were 
also prepared for comparison. Each group was tested in duplicate. Before 
the AD run, the pH in all reactors was adjusted to 7.5, the reactors were 
flushed with nitrogen to create an anaerobic environment, and then they 
were subjected to 50 days of AD at a temperature of 37 ◦C. Shaking was 
performed twice daily by hand to ensure uniform mixing. The headspace 
pressure was determined using a 3151 WAL-BMP-Test system pressure 
gauge (WAL Messund Regelsysteme GmbH, Oldenburg, Lower Saxony, 
Germany) to compute the biogas yield. Biogas volume was determined 
by Eq. (1) (Amin et al., 2021b): 
Vbiogas = ΔP × Vhead × C

2.3. Analysis methods 
The total solids (TS) and VS of tobacco straw, microbial agent, and

inoculum were tested using the APHA method, 23rd edition (APHA, 
2012). Microelements, including C, H, N, and S, were determined with a 
Vario EL CUBE element analyser (Germany). The content of O was 
computed using the formula C + H + O + N = 99.5 % on a VS basis. The 
determination of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin was based on the 
Van Soest method (Van Soest et al., 1991). The milled tobacco straw was 
determined for its lignocellulosic component, which includes neutral 
detergent fiber (NDF), acid detergent fiber (ADF) and acid detergent 
lignin (ADL). NDF and ADF determinations were fulfilled utilizing an 
ANKOM A2000i automatic fiber analyzer (ANKOM, USA) with filter 
bags. Sulfuric acid at a concentration of 72 % was added to digest the 
ADF, and the resulted residue is used to detect the ADL by the muffle 
furnace. Cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin content was calculated 
based on the interrelationship among NDF, ADF, and ADL (Surendra 
et al., 2018). The sampled digestate was centrifuged at 10000 rpm for 
10 min and then filtered using 0.45 μm and 0.22 μm filtration mem­
branes in sequence, and the resultant supernatant was used to test the 
concentration and composition of VFAs. DNA of the bacterial and 
archaeal genomes was separated from the digestate using the OMEGA 
kit. 338F (ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCA) and 806R (GGACTACH 
VGGGTWTCTAAT) were used as bacterial primers to amplify in the V3- 
V4 gene region, while 515F (GTGCCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA) and 907R 
(CCGICAATTCMTTTRAGTTT) were used as archaeal primers to amplify 
in the V4-V5 gene region. The high-quality sequences for clustering as 
operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were obtained after removing chi­
meras and non-specifically amplified sequences, based on the lowest 
similarity level of 97 %. All data were processed using Origin, Circos 
software, as well as one-way and two-way analysis of variance with a 
statistical significance threshold of 0.05.

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Methane production 
The characteristics of the substrates, inoculum, and microbial agents 
used are listed in Table 1, and according to the elemental composition, 
the MMP of tobacco straw was calculated to be 563.2 mL/g VS, which 
indicated that tobacco straw is a potential substrate for methane pro­
duction. The cumulative methane yield from AD of tobacco straw after 
the application of different microaerobic pretreatments is presented in 
Fig. 1. The cumulative methane yields of SI-0, SI-4, SI-8, SI-12, and SI-16 
were 315.9, 321.1, 257.7, 318.2, and 335.8 mL/g VS, respectively. The 
methane productions of the pretreated groups, except for the SI-8 group, 
were higher than that (298.7 mL/g VS) of the untreated tobacco straw, 
and the methane production of the SI-16 group was the highest, with an 
increase of 12.4 % compared with that of the untreated and other groups 
(*P < 0.05). From the point of view of MMP, this observation revealed 
that the SI-16 pretreatment condition might have a better capacity to 
degrade tobacco straw. Interestingly, the SI-8 group resulted in the 
lowest methane production, and there was no significant difference 
between the SI-4 and SI-12 groups (*P > 0.05). The decrease in methane 
yield in the SI-8 group compared to the untreated group might have 
occurred due to acid inhibition, and oxygen injected at concentrations of 
4 and 12 mL/g VS possibly had a similar hydrolysis effect on tobacco 
straw. As shown in Fig. 1, the methane production of the LI-pretreated 
tobacco straw fluctuated from 252.4 to 293.3 mL/g VS with varying 
oxygen concentration. Clearly, the cumulative methane yield of the LI- 
16 group was the highest, with a 5.8 % enhancement compared with 
that (277.3 mL/g VS) of the untreated group (*P < 0.05). After micro­
aerobic BS pretreatment of tobacco straw, the following EMYs were 
found: 251.7, 349.1, 294.6, 282.7, and 301.1 mL/g VS at oxygen con­
centrations of 0, 4, 8, 12, and 16 mL/g VS, respectively. BS, as a mi­
crobial pretreatment agent, resulted in better methane production in the 
microaerobic environment than under anaerobic conditions (*P < 0.05). 
The BS-4-pretreated tobacco straw showed the highest cumulative 
methane yield with an increase of 19.8 % relative to that (291.5 mL/g 
VS) of untreated straw (*P＜0.05). With increasing oxygen concentra­
tion, the methane yield of pretreated tobacco straw decreased compared 
to that of the BS-4 group (*P < 0.05). This might have occurred because 
the key facultative hydrolysis bacteria in BS, such as Enterococcus, tend 
to have good performance under low oxygen partial pressures (Tholen 
et al., 1997). 
Two-way analysis of variance was also carried out to investigate the 
effects of pretreatment types and oxygen concentrations on methane 
production of tobacco straw. The result showed that pretreatment agent 
and oxygen concentration were both the important factors to influence 
the methane production (*P < 0.01), and there was a significant inter­
action between these two factors (*P < 0.01). This result suggested that 
the effect of microaerobic pretreatment on AD was closely dependent on 
the microbial agent and oxygen concentration. Overall, it could be

concluded that LI-16, SI-16, and BS-4 had the highest methane pro­

3.2. Volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and lactic acid fluctuation after different 
microaerobic pretreatments 
The variation in the VFAs and lactic acid content due to microaerobic 
pretreatment to some extent reflects whether this technology could in­
crease hydrolysis to yield more small molecular soluble substances for 
acid production (Eryildiz et al., 2020; Valentino et al., 2021). As seen in 
Fig. 2, microaerobic pretreatment with the SI and BS agents resulted in 
higher VFAs and lactic acid production than that under anaerobic con­
dition, while only the LI agent at an oxygen concentration of 4 mL/g VS 
promoted acid production. Overall, this phenomenon might suggest that 
microaerobic conditions could enhance hydrolysis efficiency to promote 
acid accumulation. In the SI pretreatment group, acetate predominated 
at a concentration of 2640.0 mg/L in the reactor after anaerobic pre­
treatment, and its content decreased less after oxygen was injected into 
the pretreatment system. Propionate could be a valid indicator for the 
potential performance of tobacco straw hydrolysis in the pretreatment 
phase (Ohnmacht et al., 2022), and its concentrations in all micro­
aerobic reactors increased. The SI-16 group resulted in the highest 
propionate yield (1349.2 mg/L), suggesting that this condition possibly 
had a better hydrolysis performance. Lactic acid is an important indi­
cator of AD stability (Cheng et al., 2020), and high concentrations of 
lactic acid tend to hinder methanogenic microorganism activity (Bala­
sundaram et al., 2022). The average lactic acid content detected in the 
reactors with various SI pretreatments followed the order of 1900.0 mg/ 
L (SI-0) > 1700.0 mg/L (SI-8) > 1650.0 mg/L (SI-4, 12) > 1450.0 mg/L 
(SI-16). Similarly, the lactic acid content decreased in the reactor with 
various LI pretreatments along with the progressive increase in oxygen 
concentration. The content of lactic acid was relatively lower in the SI- 
16 and LI-16 groups, which might mean that the methane production 
process was less hindered, and this could be one reason why SI-16 and 
LI-16 had the highest methane production in their groups. 
Fig. 2 indicates that the acetate content in BS-0, 4, 8, 12, and 16 were 
458.2, 2386.6, 1353.0, 2292.8, and 1172.2 mg/L, respectively, and the 
highest value of 2386.6 mg/L was achieved when 4 mL/g VS oxygen was 
introduced in the BS pretreatment process. With BS-4 application, 
relatively higher production of both propionate (739.8 mg/L) and 
butyrate (6412.6 mg/L) was observed in relation to other conditions. 
The high butyrate content observed might be related to butyric acid- 
producing microorganisms such as Clostridium, but this requires 
further confirmation. On the other hand, no lactic acid was detected in 
the BS pretreatment system regardless of whether oxygen was present or 
absent. It was possible that the microorganisms in the BS possess the 
ability to convert lactic acid into acetic acid or that the rate of lactic acid 
production did not match its conversion rate. It could be seen that BS-4 
pretreatment had the ability to produce more intermediate acids for

3.3. Microstructural analysis 
Microbial pretreatments via the injection of optimal concentrations 
of oxygen (SI-16, LI-16, BS-4) may influence the physicochemical and 
structural properties of tobacco straw; therefore, FTIR and XRD moni­
toring were performed to observe structure changes in this study (see 
supplementary material). 
Infrared absorption spectra, one indicator of functional groups, could 
be applied to discover the relative digestibility of the lignocellulose in 
tobacco straw. Tobacco straw with and without optimal microaerobic 
pretreatment was quite different, indicating major differences and 
overlap in the spectral regions assigned to the tensile vibrations of –OH 
in lignocellulose (3323.0 cm−1), stretching vibrations of the CH3-CO– 
group in hemicellulose (1734.0 cm−1), tensile and skeletal vibrations of 
C––C in the aromatic ring of lignin (1626.0 cm−1, 1510.0 cm−1), 
asymmetric stretching vibration of C-O-C in cellulose and C-O stretching 
vibrations of cellulose and hemicellulose (1155.0 cm−1, 1054.0 cm−1) 
(Kumar et al., 2019; Taherdanak and Zilouei, 2014). The transmittance 
rates at 3323.0–3418.0 cm−1, 1734.0 cm−1, 1155.0 cm−1, and 1054.0 
cm−1 were in the order BS-4 > SI-16 > LI-16 > untreated; the trans­
mittance rates at 1626.0 and 1510.0 cm−1 were in the order SI-16 > LI-

16 > BS-4 > untreated. In general, the lower the transmittance band is, 
the stronger the absorbance. In other words, the higher transmittance 
bands at 3323.0–3418.0 cm−1, 1734.0 cm−1, 1155.0 cm−1, and 1054.0 
cm−1 of the BS-4-pretreated tobacco straw meant that the weaker 
absorbance for the cellulose and hemicellulose, suggesting a stronger 
decomposition in terms of cellulose and hemicellulose. Accordingly, the 
transmittance band from BS-4 pretreated tobacco straw assigned to 
lignin was relatively lower, and thus, the relative absorbance attributed 
to lignin was higher than that from the other pretreatment conditions, 
which might be due to the relative content of lignin increased as the 
decomposition of cellulose and hemicellulose. The introduction of 4 mL/ 
g VS in the BS pretreatment process might have a better hydrolysis 
performance for cellulose and hemicellulose, and therefore resulted in 
the highest methane production in this study. 
The identification and quantification of the crystallinity and amor­
phous phase in tobacco straw were performed utilizing XRD (see sup­
plementary material). Given the XRD data, the calculated order of 
cellulose crystallinity was BS-4 (29.9 %) > SI-16 (28.6 %) > untreated 
(17.3 %) > LI-16 (17.1 %), among which untreated and LI-16 tobacco 
straw were insignificantly different in the CrI. BS-4 and SI-16 contrib­
uted to the strengthening of CrI, exhibiting a higher relative content of 
cellulose primarily in the crystal state. The underlying reason for this 
might be that cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin in the amorphous re­
gion were significantly decomposed, which resulted in an increase in the 
relative content of cellulose in the crystalline form. 
3.4. Kinetic analysis 
A modified Gompertz model was utilized to serve as an important 
reference for understanding the different AD processes in this study. The 
kinetic curve and fitted parameters of all the reactions were computed 
by a statistical algorithm, and model sensitivity was analysed compare 
the experimental results and the simulated values; the fit was considered 
good at an R2 value over 0.98 as shown in Table 2. λ is associated with 
the lag period of the process, and its values for BS-4, SI-16, and LI-16 are 
12.3, 12.8, and 10.9, respectively. In comparison, the lag period of BS-4 
did not significantly differ from that of SI-16 and was higher than that of 
LI-16. However, the gap between BS-4 and LI-16 in the lag period might 
have been compensated by the higher methane production in the BS-4 
group. For the maximum methane production, all Y0 results are signif­
icantly close to the experimental methane production. BS-4 pretreat­
ment showed the most effective lignocellulose decomposition, as it had 
the highest BD value of 61.9 %, followed by 59.6 % in BS-16 pretreated 
straw, further showing good agreement with the methane production 
analysis above. 
3.5. Microbial analysis 
3.5.1. Bacterial composition at the genus level 
The bacterial composition of the three microbial agents as well as 
that in the reactors prior and after optimal pretreatment and AD process 
is shown at the genus level in Fig. 3. The top 2 bacterial genera with high 
abundance in SI were Bacillus and Streptomyces, with relative abun­
dances of 60.6 % and 13.7 %, respectively. Bacillus, a strictly aerobic or 
facultative anaerobic bacterium affiliated with Firmicutes, is responsible 
for the hydrolysis of large lignocellulosic molecules into soluble sugars 
(Wang et al., 2021; Zabed et al., 2019), and its relative abundances were 
3.0 % and 0.9 % after SI-0 and SI-16 pretreatment, respectively, and 
then changed to negligible level at the end of AD. The FTIR results 
indicated that the peaks associated with cellulose, hemicellulose, and 
lignin all decreased in pretreated tobacco straw with SI compared with 
untreated tobacco straw. The reason behind this result might be that 
Bacillus could secrete a variety of enzymes (e.g., cellulase, xylanase, 
amylase, peroxidase) and thus promote lignocellulose dissolution during 
pretreatment stage. Streptomyces, a bacterium belonging to the phylum 
Actinomycetes, is widely present in soils and plays an important role in 
the degradation of organic matter (Hong et al., 2010). The relative 
abundances of Streptomyces were 0.3 % and 0.1 % after SI-0 and SI-16 
pretreatment with insignificant difference between them, and after 
AD, this bacterium was hardly detected. It could secrete a lytic poly­
saccharide monooxygenase, which was initially found to degrade chitin 
and later was shown to destroy the glycosidic bond of cellulose. Lytic 
polysaccharide monooxygenase primarily decomposes refractory poly­
saccharides in the crystalline zone of lignocellulose through oxidation 
and results in the generation of oxidized oligosaccharides (Hong et al., 
2010). Additionally, this enzyme could work with hydrolase to increase 
the hydrolysis efficiency of lignocellulose (Eibinger et al., 2014; Sharma 
et al., 2019), which might promote the degradation of lignocellulose. At 
the same time, there is significant increases in the relative abundance of 
Lactobacillus from 2 % in the SI to 30.6 % and 60.0 % in the SI-0 and SI- 
16 pretreatment processes, respectively. At the end of AD, the relative 
abundance of Lactobacillus was reduced to a negligible level. Lactoba­
cillus belong to the family Lactobacillaceae, among which anaerobic,

the hydrolysis and acidification process (D’ Silva et al., 2021), with 
functions involving the fermentation of sugar to release acetic and lactic 
acid for bacterial development and subsequent methanogenesis. 
Therefore, the higher relative abundance of Lactobacillus in SI-16 pre­
treatment process was probably resulted from the increasing facultative 
microorganisms in the genus Lactobacillus, and this was consistent with 
the result of Nguyen et al. (2019) who also found microaerobic condi­
tion was good for the enrichment of facultative bacterium. Based on the 
microbial community analysis, optimal oxygen injection in SI pretreat­
ment process could significantly enhance the relative abundance of 
facultative bacterium in genus Lactobacillus, and then produce more 
acetic and lactic acid, which was likely to be the explanation for the 
increase in methane production with SI-16 pretreatment application. 
Among the LI agents, Lactobacillus and Lactococcus were the top 2 
bacteria, with relative abundances of 45.3 % and 41.1 %, respectively. 
Both genera belong to Firmicutes and are responsible for lactic acid 
production with sugars as the carbon nutrients (McAteer et al., 2020; 
Wang et al., 2021). The relative abundances of Lactobacillus were 73.5 % 
and 43.5 % after LI-0 and LI-16 pretreatment, respectively. A possible 
reason for this phenomenon was that anaerobic microorganisms in the 
genus Lactobacillus in the LI agent treatment were likely to be predom­
inant. The excessive higher abundance of this bacterium in anaerobic 
pretreatment environment might induce acid accumulation, and there­
fore had a negative effect on methane production, which could be the 
reason why LI-16 had higher methane production than that of LI-0. 
Weissella was not the main genus (0.4 %) in LI and accounted for 
higher proportions at the end of LI-0 (12.8 %) and LI-16 pretreatment 
(23.0 %), and it was hard to be detected in AD stage. Weissella is a 
facultative anaerobe that belongs to Firmicutes, which could digest car­
bohydrate through the hexose-monophosphate and the phosphoketolase 
pathways to produce acetate and ethanol (Fusco et al., 2015). 
Additionally, Enterobacter was enriched to 12.7 % in the LI-16 pre­
treatment process relative to that of 5.8 % in LI-0 condition, which was 
reported to have special ligninolytic species such as Enterobacter hor­
maechei KA3 (Zhang et al., 2021). Upon the optimal dosing of oxygen for 
the LI pretreatment process, the digestion of carbohydrate in tobacco 
straw was facilitated via abovementioned pathway from Weissella. At 
the same time, the increase in the relative abundance of Enterobacter 
might play an important role in lignin degradation, and this result was 
consistent with the FTIR analysis, which suggested that LI-16 had a 
weaker absorption strength for lignin than untreated. As a whole, 
optimal oxygen loaded in LI pretreatment process could help the 
fermentation of carbohydrate and lignin, and therefore enhance the 
methane production. 
In terms of BS, Lactobacillus in BS increased from 0.25 % to 6.4 % and 
14.8 % in the BS-0 and BS-4 pretreatment environments, respectively. As 
mentioned above, Lactobacillus in BS-4 pretreatment process was iden­
tified as a functional microorganism for yielding acetic and lactic acid, 
and in contrast with the SI and LI groups, the significantly lower average 
abundance of Lactobacillus might have resulted in less lactic acid pro­
duction in pretreatment process. Clostridium sensu stricto 12 showed a 
higher relative abundance of 8.1 % in BS-4 pretreatment process than 
that of 6.1 % under BS-0 condition, and it is a common bacterium that 
carries out hydrolysis to produce acetic and butyric acid (Zhao et al., 
2022). Interestingly, the pH under this microaerobic environment was 
approximately 6, showing good agreement with the findings of Zhao 
et al. (2021) who found that Clostridium sensu stricto 12 was capable of 
hydrolysing organic substances into butyric acid at pH = 6. This finding 
was consistent with the proposed reason for the high butyrate produc­
tion, as mentioned in the VFAs analysis. Enterococcus, a facultative 
genus, was enriched in both the anaerobic and microaerobic pretreat­
ment phases. Tholen et al. (1997) found that Enterococcus could increase

oxygen pressure. Hence, the BS microaerobic pretreatment system might 
have two characteristics: the first was to rapidly consume the accumu­
lated lactic acid to produce acetic acid under relative lower oxygen 
concentration, and the second was to increase the relative abundance of 
genus Clostridium sensu stricto 12 for enhancing hydrolysis rate. This 
might be a reason that the lowest oxygen concentration of 4 mL/g VS 
under pretreatment process was better to increase the methane pro­
duction when BS was used as microbial agent. 
3.5.2. Archaeal composition at the genus level 
The archaeal composition analysis at the genus level revealed that 
Methnanobacterium, Candidatus Methanoplasma, Metanomassilicoccus, 
Metanobrevibacter, Methanosarcina, and Methanosaeta were present at the 
end of AD (Fig. 4). Among them, in addition to unassigned archaea, 
Methanobacterium and Candidatus Methanoplasma were the most abun­
dant genera. Methanobacterium, in the family Methanobacteriaceae, is 
involved in the transformation of carbon dioxide and hydrogen into 
methane (Amin et al., 2021a). As for SI pretreatment group, Meth­
anobacterium was more abundant in the SI-0 (3.3 %) than that of SI-16 
(1.3 %), suggesting a dominated hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis 
might occur on anaerobic environment. In terms of LI pretreatment 
group, the relative abundances of Methanobacterium from LI-0 and LI-16 
were 0.8 % and 2.6 %, respectively. This phenomenon was opposed to 
that in SI group, indicating that oxygen might promote hydro­
genotrophic methanogenesis in this system. At the end of AD of BS 
group, there is no significant difference between BS-0 (1.4 %) and BS-4 
(1.2 %) groups. These results showed that the change of archaeal genus 
might be varied with the pretreatment agent and oxygen concentration, 
which showed a good accordance with the previous two-way analysis 
result. Candidatus Methanoplasma is believed to use methyl compounds 
such as methanol, hydrogen, and carbon dioxide for methane synthesis 
(Vendruscolo et al., 2020). The relative abundances of SI-0 and SI-16 
were 7.0 % and 3.0 %, respectively, and Candidatus Methanoplasma 
was rarely found in the AD process with LI as the microbial agent. A 
higher abundance (1.3 %) of the archaeal genus Candidatus Meth­
anoplasma was observed in BS-16 than in BS-0 (0.2 %), and this indi­
cated that the presence of oxygen in pretreatment step using BS might be 
good for methanogenesis process. 
4. Conclusions 
The pretreatment of tobacco straw via BS application as a microbial 
agent at an oxygen concentration of 4 mL/g VS resulted in the greatest 
increase in VFAs and methane production. This might occur due to the 
high relative abundance of Enterococcus and Clostridium sensu stricto 12 
in the pretreatment phase, which led to better hydrolysation of ligno­
cellulose. In AD, Candidatus Methanoplasma, which can transform most 
of methyl compounds into methane, might also be a reason for the su­
perior methane production under this condition. This study advances 
the understanding of microaerobic pretreatment and offers valuable 
guidelines to effectively utilize tobacco straw.
